extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of humor; comedy theorists and writers interested in theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Critchley's model of humor as a double movement that both reaffirms a community's shared sensus communis and defamiliarizes it; use the model to analyze or produce jokes that engage bodily, mortal, or mechanical themes and that are ethically liberating. Suitable for theoretical analysis or informed comedic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation: reliance on a shared sensus communis
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke depends on a shared background of expectations, norms, and cultural meaning; the joke recalls us to 'common sense' — to what we, as a community, take for granted. Without shared sensus communis, the joke can't land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke presupposes a recognizable set of assumptions, references, or norms that the audience must share. Examples: in-group references, shared cultural assumptions. Anti-pattern: implicit references that an intended audience does not possess, producing incomprehension rather than laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departure: defamiliarization / dissensus communis
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke estranges us from what we take for granted; it defamiliarizes the everyday by showing it from a strange angle and 'explodes the sheer arbitrariness of social rites' through 'miniature strategies of defamiliarization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which the joke disrupts ordinary expectations or reveals arbitrariness in social practices. Examples: perspective shifts, incongruous juxtapositions, reframing routines as absurd. Anti-pattern: mere restatement of shared norms without any estrangement (no comic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double movement: coexistence of return and departure
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a paradoxical double character: it both reaffirms the shared world and explodes that common sense from within. The two movements coexist in the same comic act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the joke both relies on shared norms and simultaneously defamiliarizes them, within a single comic act. Scoring note: successful jokes balance affirmation and disruption; purely affirming or purely alienating acts fail to achieve Critchley-style comic closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition — shared sensus communis (explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a shared sensus communis between speaker and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a precondition check: confirm the intended audience and performer share enough contextual knowledge and normative background for the joke's references to function. If absent, the joke will not 'land' as Critchley describes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition — movement of departure
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke must defamiliarize, not merely affirm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for elements that destabilize or make strange the taken-for-granted. Anti-pattern: jokes that only restate or celebrate shared norms without any rupturing insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition — return to common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke must remain within the community's grasp; total alienation produces incomprehension. There must be a return after departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether, after the disruptive moment, the audience can reestablish shared understanding and laugh together. If the joke leaves the audience alienated rather than reintegrated, it fails Critchley's model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition — reference to a core source (body, mortality, mechanical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke should reference one of Critchley's three core human anxieties — the animal body, mortality, or the mechanical — to give the joke human weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the material taps into bodily realities (sex, digestion, decay), mortality (death, illness, aging), or the mechanical (repetitive, machine-like behaviour). A connection to one of these grounds the humor in shared human vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core source — our animal body
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at the body, at bodily functions, at the contrast between our self-image as rational and our reality as fleshy creatures (food, sex, digestion, breath, decay; pretentious behaviour collapsing into bodily inelegance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or crafting jokes, note uses of corporeal incongruity, degradation of pretension into the bodily, slapstick, or scatological elements. Ethical note: using bodily material to invite collective self-recognition is preferable to targeting specific individuals to humiliate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core source — our mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at death, at memento mori, at the gap between our lifeplans and our certain end (gallows humor; jokes about funerals, illness, aging; pretensions of the living against dying).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the joke exposes human finitude and the leveling effect of death; examples include gallows humor and irony about aging. Evaluate ethical stance: does it invite shared recognition of vulnerability or does it exploit others' suffering?

rubrics_metrics.name: Core source — the mechanical (resemblance to machines)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when the human reveals itself as machine-like: repetitive behavior, predictable responses, inflexibility where flexibility was needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify comedic targets that highlight automatism, rigidity, and mechanical repetition. Bergsonian echoes: parodying routinized behaviour can produce laughter by revealing the non-human aspects of human conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical humor: liberating shared humanity vs cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest humor is ethical: it draws attention to our common condition and invites us to laugh together at 'us' rather than mocking specific others. This laughter is liberating because it undoes pretension and reaffirms shared humanity. It differs from the cruelty of mere mockery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging humor, distinguish between inclusive self-directed laughter that undermines pretension and exclusive, cruel mockery that targets outsiders. Prefer techniques that invite collective recognition and mitigate humiliation of particular groups or individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-building function and social diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Because humor depends on sensus communis, communities define themselves partly by what they find funny; sharing a sense of humor signals belonging. A joke that fails marks failure of shared background — it's socially diagnostic. Outsiders often can't access in-group humor; mastery of the group's humor is mastery of its world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor as a lens for social belonging: analyze who laughs, who doesn't, and what that reveals about group boundaries. Anti-pattern: assuming universality of a joke's references; recognize humor as an index of inclusion/exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist (questions for evaluating a joke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five analytic questions: What sensus communis does the joke presuppose? Where does it depart from / defamiliarize that shared world? Does it return — does the audience come back to common sense after the comic departure? Does it touch on body, mortality, or the mechanical? Is the laughter ethical (liberating shared humanity) or cruel (mocking outsiders)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these questions as a practical evaluation tool when analyzing or composing jokes. Use them to check preconditions, the presence of the double movement, grounding in one of the three sources, and the ethical valence of the laughter. They function as an operational rubric for Critchley-style humor.
